stem: In paper chromatography, why is the base line drawn in pencil rather than in ink?

options.content: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent; ink would run.
options.rationale: Graphite is insoluble, so it stays put.

options.content: Pencil lines are easier to rub out once the run has finished.
options.rationale: Being able to erase it is not the reason.

options.content: Ink would make the paper too wet to use.
options.rationale: The problem is that ink dissolves and runs.

options.content: Pencil helps the solvent move up the paper.
options.rationale: The line has no effect on how the solvent moves.

explanation: Ink contains dyes that dissolve in the solvent; they would move up the paper and add extra spots. Pencil marks are graphite, which is insoluble, so the line stays where it is.

stem: Why must the level of the solvent be **below** the base line at the start of paper chromatography?

options.content: Otherwise the spots would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.
options.rationale: The samples must be carried up the paper by the solvent.

options.content: Otherwise the wet paper would soften and tear at the solvent level.
options.rationale: Wet paper does not tear at the solvent level.

options.content: Otherwise the solvent could not move up the paper.
options.rationale: Solvent moves up the paper whatever the level.

options.content: Otherwise the pencil base line would dissolve away.
options.rationale: Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve.

explanation: If the spots were below the solvent surface, they would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker and be lost. With the base line above the solvent, the solvent soaks up past the spots and carries them up the paper.

stem: True or false: a pure substance gives only one spot on a chromatogram.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: a single substance gives a single spot; a mixture gives more than one.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: a pure substance contains only one substance, so it gives one spot.

explanation: A pure substance contains only one substance, so it gives a single spot. Two or more spots show a mixture.

stem: A green food colouring gives three separate spots on a chromatogram. What does this show?

options.content: It is a mixture of at least three substances.
options.rationale: Each spot is a different substance.

options.content: It is a pure substance.
options.rationale: A pure substance gives only one spot.

options.content: It contains exactly one green dye that has split up.
options.rationale: Three spots mean at least three substances.

options.content: The solvent was the wrong colour.
options.rationale: The solvent does not form spots.

explanation: Each spot is a different soluble substance, so the colouring is a mixture of at least three substances. (It may contain more if any are insoluble in the solvent or have the same Rf.)

stem: **Supplement.** Complete the definition of the Rf value.

payload.template: The Rf value equals the distance moved by the {{blank:top}} divided by the distance moved by the {{blank:bottom}}, both measured from the base line.

explanation: $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent}}$, both from the base line. It is always between 0 and 1.

stem: **Supplement.** On a chromatogram the solvent front is $9.0\ \text{cm}$ above the base line, and the centre of a red spot is $2.7\ \text{cm}$ above the base line. Calculate the Rf value of the red substance.
workedSolution:
1. $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}$.
2. $R_f = \dfrac{2.7}{9.0} = 0.30$ (no units).
hints: Divide the spot's distance by the solvent's distance.

stem: **Supplement.** A dye has an Rf value of $0.65$ in ethanol. On a chromatogram run in ethanol, the solvent front is $6.0\ \text{cm}$ above the base line. How far above the base line will the centre of the dye's spot be?
explanation: Distance moved by the dye $= R_f \times$ distance moved by the solvent $= 0.65 \times 6.0 = 3.9\ \text{cm}$.
workedSolution:
1. Rearrange: distance moved by substance $= R_f \times$ distance moved by solvent.
2. $= 0.65 \times 6.0 = 3.9\ \text{cm}$.
hints: Rearrange the Rf equation to find the distance moved by the substance.

stem: **Supplement.** Which of these could **not** be an Rf value?

options.rationale: An Rf value above 1 would mean the substance moved further than the solvent, which is impossible.
A substance that is only slightly soluble moves a short distance: a small Rf is possible.
The substance moved half as far as the solvent.
A very soluble substance moves almost as far as the solvent.

explanation: A substance is carried by the solvent, so it can never travel further than the solvent front. Rf values are therefore always between 0 and 1.
hints: Can a substance move further than the solvent that carries it?

stem: **Supplement.** Amino acids are colourless. After separating a mixture of amino acids by paper chromatography, how can their positions be shown?

options.content: Draw the base line in ink so that the spots are coloured.
options.rationale: Ink would dissolve and add its own dyes; it would not colour the amino acids.

options.content: Dry it and spray it with a locating agent to make coloured spots.
options.rationale: Locating agents react with colourless substances to make them visible.

options.content: Run the chromatogram for longer until colours appear.
options.rationale: Running it longer does not make colourless spots visible.

options.content: Add a coloured dye to the solvent before running it.
options.rationale: A dyed solvent would colour the whole paper, not the spots.

explanation: Colourless substances are revealed by spraying the dried chromatogram with a locating agent, which reacts with them to give coloured spots. (Some substances can instead be seen under ultraviolet light.) Their Rf values can then be measured.
hints: Something has to react with the amino acids to make them visible.

stem: Match each chromatography term with its meaning. One meaning is not used.

right.content: The pencil line on which the samples are placed
The furthest point reached by the solvent
The dried paper showing the separated substances
Shows that the sample is probably pure
Shows that the solvent was contaminated

explanation: The base line is the pencil start line; the solvent front is how far the solvent travelled; the chromatogram is the finished, dried paper; a single spot suggests a pure substance.

stem: Name the method used to separate the different coloured dyes in a sample of black ink.

rejected.feedback: Dissolved dyes pass through filter paper. Chromatography separates them.
Distillation separates liquids or a solvent. Dissolved dyes are separated by chromatography.

explanation: Chromatography separates small amounts of dissolved substances such as the dyes in ink: each dye travels a different distance up the paper.

stem:
A food scientist tests the orange colouring from a freezit, X, against four permitted food dyes, A, B, C and D, using water as the solvent. The solvent front is $10.0\ \text{cm}$ above the base line.

| Sample | Heights of spots above the base line / cm |
| --- | --- |
| X | 0 (on the base line), 3.0, 7.5 |
| A | 3.0 |
| B | 5.0 |
| C | 7.5 |
| D | 9.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the smallest number of different substances in X?

options.rationale: The spot left on the base line is a substance too.
Several spots show that X is a mixture.
Two spots moved and one stayed on the base line: three substances.
Only three spots are seen.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Select **all** the permitted dyes that X contains.

options.content: A
options.rationale: X has a spot at 3.0 cm, like A.

options.content: B
options.rationale: X has no spot at 5.0 cm.

options.content: C
options.rationale: X has a spot at 7.5 cm, like C.

options.content: D
options.rationale: X has no spot at 9.0 cm.

options.content: None of A, B, C and D
options.rationale: Two of the spots of X match permitted dyes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: **Supplement.** Calculate the Rf value of dye C.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: One substance in X stayed on the base line. What does this show, and how could the scientist find out more about it?

points.description: It is insoluble in water (the solvent used)
Run the chromatogram again with a different solvent (in which it dissolves), alongside other reference substances

parts.explanation: The substance on the base line is insoluble in water, so it did not move. The scientist could repeat the chromatography with a different solvent, such as ethanol, in which it dissolves, and compare it with other known substances.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Do the results show that X contains only permitted dyes?

options.content: Yes: every spot of X matches one of the permitted dyes.
options.rationale: The base-line spot does not match A, B, C or D.

options.content: Yes: X contains permitted dye D and no other dye at all.
options.rationale: X has no spot at 9.0 cm.

options.content: No: X contains dye B, which is not on the permitted list.
options.rationale: X has no spot at 5.0 cm.

options.content: No: one spot matches no permitted dye, so more tests are needed.
options.rationale: One component of X has not been identified.

explanation: X gives three spots (one on the base line), so it contains at least three substances. Its spots at 3.0 cm and 7.5 cm match dyes A and C. Dye C: $R_f = \dfrac{7.5}{10.0} = 0.75$. The base-line substance is insoluble in water and matches no permitted dye, so it must be investigated with another solvent.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** 3.
2. **(b)** A and C.
3. **(c)** $\dfrac{7.5}{10.0} = 0.75$.
4. **(d)** It is insoluble in water; repeat with a different solvent.
5. **(e)** No: the base-line substance is unidentified.
hints: Count every spot, including any on the base line.
Match the heights of X's spots with the reference dyes.

stem: An unknown dye and a known dye give spots at the same height when run in water. How could a chemist be more confident that they are the same substance?

options.content: Run them again in water on a longer piece of paper and compare the heights.
options.rationale: The same solvent would give the same result: it adds no new evidence.

options.content: Run them again in a different solvent and check the spots still match.
options.rationale: Two different substances rarely match in two different solvents.

options.content: Draw the base line in ink instead of pencil this time.
options.rationale: Ink would add extra spots.

options.content: Measure the spots again with a more accurate ruler.
options.rationale: They already match; a different solvent is a better test.

explanation: Two different substances can occasionally have the same Rf in one solvent. If they still match in a second, different solvent, it is very likely they are the same substance.
hints: What could change the result if the substances were different?

stem: Why is a lid placed on the beaker during paper chromatography?

options.content: To stop light from fading the dyes during the long run.
options.rationale: The run takes only minutes; light is not the issue.

options.content: So the air is saturated and solvent does not evaporate from the paper.
options.rationale: This lets the solvent move steadily up the paper.

options.content: To keep the paper warm so that the dyes dissolve better in the solvent.
options.rationale: The lid is about solvent evaporation, not temperature.

options.content: To stop the paper from falling down into the solvent below.
options.rationale: The paper is held by a clip or rod, not by the lid.

explanation: Covering the beaker keeps the air inside saturated with solvent vapour. Less solvent evaporates from the paper, so it moves up steadily and the spots separate well.

stem: True or false: in thin-layer chromatography (TLC), the substances move up a thin layer of a solid, such as silica gel, coated on a plate, instead of up a sheet of paper.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: TLC uses a plate coated with a thin layer of silica gel (or a similar solid).
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: the paper is replaced by a glass, plastic or aluminium plate coated with a thin layer of silica gel.

explanation: In TLC the paper is replaced by a plate coated with a thin layer of a solid such as silica gel. The method is otherwise the same: pencil base line, small spots, solvent below the line, lid and solvent front.

stem: What is an advantage of thin-layer chromatography (TLC) over paper chromatography?

options.content: It does not need a solvent to move the spots.
options.rationale: TLC needs a solvent, just like paper chromatography.

options.content: It is faster and gives sharper, better-separated spots.
options.rationale: That is why TLC is widely used to check medicines.

options.content: It can separate substances that are insoluble.
options.rationale: Substances must dissolve in the solvent to move.

options.content: It gives Rf values greater than 1 for every dye.
options.rationale: No substance can move further than the solvent, so an Rf value is never greater than 1, in TLC or on paper.

explanation: TLC runs faster, gives sharper and better-separated spots and can be used with a wider range of solvents.
hints: Think about speed and how clear the spots are.

stem: A brand of orange drink may contain a banned dye, D. A sample of pure D is available. Describe how you would use paper chromatography to find out whether the drink contains D. [6]

points.description: Draw a base line in pencil about 1.5–2 cm from the bottom of the chromatography paper
Put small, concentrated spots of the drink (colouring) and of pure D side by side on the base line
Stand the paper in a suitable solvent with the solvent level below the base line
Cover with a lid and leave until the solvent has nearly reached the top
Remove the paper, mark the solvent front and let it dry
If one of the drink's spots is at the same height as D (same Rf) the drink probably contains D; if no spot matches, D is absent

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Draw a **pencil** line about 2 cm from the bottom of a piece of chromatography paper. Using a capillary tube, put a small, concentrated spot of the drink's colouring and, beside it, a spot of pure dye D on the line. Stand the paper in a beaker containing a little solvent (for example water), with the solvent **below the base line**, and cover the beaker. When the solvent has almost reached the top, remove the paper, **mark the solvent front** in pencil and let it dry.

Compare the spots. If one of the spots from the drink is at the **same height** as the spot of D (the same Rf value), the drink probably contains D. If none of its spots match, D is not present.

explanation: A correct set-up (pencil base line, solvent below it, lid, solvent front) and a clear comparison with pure D are both needed.
hints: Run the drink and pure D side by side on the same paper.

stem:
**Supplement.** A protein is broken down into its amino acids, which are separated by paper chromatography. The dry chromatogram is sprayed with a locating agent. The solvent front is $10.0\ \text{cm}$ above the base line, and two spots appear at $2.0\ \text{cm}$ and $5.5\ \text{cm}$ above the base line. The table gives Rf values of four amino acids in the same solvent.

| Amino acid | A | B | C | D |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rf value | 0.20 | 0.35 | 0.55 | 0.70 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why is a locating agent used?

options.content: It makes the solvent move faster up the paper.
options.rationale: It is sprayed on after the chromatogram has dried.

options.content: It breaks the protein down into its separate amino acids.
options.rationale: That happens before the chromatography.

options.content: Amino acids are colourless, so it makes their spots visible.
options.rationale: It reacts with them to form coloured spots.

options.content: It removes the solvent front from the paper after drying.
options.rationale: The solvent front is marked in pencil before spraying.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the Rf value of the spot $2.0\ \text{cm}$ above the base line.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the Rf value of the spot $5.5\ \text{cm}$ above the base line.

options.content: A
options.rationale: Rf 0.20 matches A.

options.content: B
options.rationale: No spot has Rf 0.35.

options.content: C
options.rationale: Rf 0.55 matches C.

options.content: D
options.rationale: No spot has Rf 0.70.

options.content: None of A, B, C and D
options.rationale: Both Rf values match amino acids in the table.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Why must the chromatogram be run in the same solvent as the one used for the table?

options.content: Different solvents give Rf values above 1.
options.rationale: Rf values are never greater than 1, whatever the solvent: no substance moves further than the solvent front.

options.content: The locating agent only works in that solvent.
options.rationale: The reason is that Rf depends on the solvent.

options.content: A substance's Rf value depends on the solvent.
options.rationale: The same substance has different Rf values in different solvents.

options.content: Other solvents dissolve the paper.
options.rationale: Chromatography solvents do not dissolve the paper.

explanation: The amino acids are colourless, so a locating agent reveals them. $R_f = \dfrac{2.0}{10.0} = 0.20$ (amino acid A) and $\dfrac{5.5}{10.0} = 0.55$ (amino acid C). Rf values can only be compared for the same solvent, because the Rf of a substance depends on the solvent.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** The amino acids are colourless.
2. **(b)** $\dfrac{2.0}{10.0} = 0.20$.
3. **(c)** $\dfrac{5.5}{10.0} = 0.55$.
4. **(d)** A and C.
5. **(e)** Rf depends on the solvent.
hints: Divide each spot's distance by 10.0 cm.
Compare your Rf values with the table.

stem: **Supplement.** The base line on a chromatogram is $2.0\ \text{cm}$ above the bottom edge of the paper. The centre of a spot is $5.0\ \text{cm}$ above the bottom edge, and the solvent front is $10.0\ \text{cm}$ above the bottom edge. What is the Rf value of the spot?

options.rationale: This uses distances from the bottom edge ($5.0 \div 10.0$); they must be measured from the base line.
$3.0 \div 10.0$ measures the spot from the base line but the solvent from the edge.
$5.0 \div 8.0$ mixes the two starting points the other way round.

explanation: Both distances must be measured from the base line: the spot moved $5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0\ \text{cm}$ and the solvent $10.0 - 2.0 = 8.0\ \text{cm}$, so $R_f = \dfrac{3.0}{8.0} = 0.375$.
hints: Subtract the height of the base line from both measurements first.

stem: **Supplement.** Rudo grinds covo leaves with a little sand and propanone, then spots the green extract on chromatography paper and runs it in a suitable solvent. Four pigments separate: an orange-yellow pigment P, a yellow pigment Q, a blue-green pigment R and a yellow-green pigment S. The solvent front is $12.0\ \text{cm}$ above the base line, and the centre of the spot of P is $10.8\ \text{cm}$ above the base line.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why are the leaves ground with sand and propanone?

options.content: To make the pigments react with the sand and change colour
options.rationale: Grinding is a physical process; the pigments are not changed.

options.content: To remove the pigments that are insoluble in water
options.rationale: The aim is to dissolve as much pigment as possible.

options.content: To make the extract colourless before it is spotted
options.rationale: The extract is green because it contains the pigments.

options.content: To break open the cells so the pigments dissolve in the propanone
options.rationale: The pigments are inside the cells and dissolve in propanone.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the Rf value of pigment P.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Pigment P travels the furthest. What does this suggest about P?

options.content: It is the least soluble of the pigments in this solvent.
options.rationale: A substance of low solubility moves only a short distance.

options.content: It is insoluble in this solvent and is pushed up.
options.rationale: An insoluble substance would stay on the base line.

options.content: It is present in the largest amount in the leaves.
options.rationale: Distance depends on solubility, not on amount.

options.content: It is the most soluble of the four pigments in this solvent.
options.rationale: The more soluble a substance, the further the solvent carries it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Pigment R has an Rf value of $0.40$ in this solvent. How far above the base line is its spot?

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: On another chromatogram, the spots of Q and S overlap. Suggest **two** ways of improving the separation.

points.description: Any one: use a different solvent (in which Q and S have different Rf values); use a longer piece of paper / let the solvent travel further
Any one different: use smaller, more concentrated spots; use thin-layer chromatography (sharper separation)

parts.explanation: Use a different solvent in which Q and S have different Rf values, or let the solvent run further up a longer paper. Smaller, more concentrated spots, or thin-layer chromatography, would also give sharper, better-separated spots.

explanation: Grinding with sand and propanone breaks the cells and dissolves the pigments. $R_f(\text{P}) = \dfrac{10.8}{12.0} = 0.90$: P is the most soluble pigment in this solvent, so it travels furthest. R moves $0.40 \times 12.0 = 4.8\ \text{cm}$. Overlapping spots can be separated better with a different solvent, a longer run, smaller spots or TLC.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** To break the cells and dissolve the pigments.
2. **(b)** $\dfrac{10.8}{12.0} = 0.90$.
3. **(c)** P is the most soluble in the solvent.
4. **(d)** $0.40 \times 12.0 = 4.8\ \text{cm}$.
5. **(e)** For example: a different solvent; a longer run; smaller spots.
hints: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent.
Rearrange the Rf equation for part (d).
